INTR5100 Lab Session I — IDM Calibration and Validation

Driver driver_1 · identified with method M5 · validation run: present
DEMO REPORT. DEMO - no validation run exists yet. The validation tables of this report come from the human collection data/raw/collection_20260917_144342 (the other driver's recording), pushed through the same stage 1..4 pipeline as if it were the driver_1 validation run. The preprocessing, the IDM replay, the metrics and the figures are the real code paths; only the role of the validation input is simulated, so the model-transfer error visible in section 4 is expected (the parameters of driver_1 are being applied to a trajectory it was never fitted to) and is not a defect of the pipeline. The numbers are computed by the real pipeline on the real files; only the role of the validation input is simulated.
How to produce this report. One command does the whole job once the validation collection exists (a directory with the same layout as a human collection, i.e. straight_trajectory.csv):
python src/run_validation_pipeline.py --validation-raw <collections-dir> --driver driver_1 --report
The two steps can also be run separately:
python src/run_validation_pipeline.py --validation-raw <collections-dir> --driver driver_1
python src/analysis/build_html_report.py --driver driver_1
The pipeline writes data/preprocess/validation_<driver>/stage_1..4 and results/validation_driver_1.json; the report generator reads those artifacts and writes results/lab1_full_report.html.
1. Experiment and model · 2. Data processing · 3. Calibration · 4. Validation · 5. Driving style · 6. Limitations

1. Experiment and model

A human driver follows a leader vehicle along the straight sections of a closed test route. The collected trajectories are cleaned and merged into per-event tables (time, fv, lv, dhw) and an Intelligent Driver Model (IDM) is fitted to driver_1's driving with five different identification methods. The winning parameter vector is used in a TA-driven validation run on the same route; this report compares the validation data with the human data and with the model's reproduction of both.

aIDM(s, v, Δv) = a · [ 1 − (v/v0)δ − (s*/s)2 ]
s* = s0 + max(0, v·T + v·Δv / (2√(a·b)))   Δv = vleader − v
ds/dt = vleader − v    dv/dt = aIDM(s, v, Δv)    s = dhw − LVEH, LVEH = 250 cu, δ = 4 (fixed)

The leader is an input rather than a state: the simulation starts from the first measured sample of the event and is fed the measured leader speed at every integration node, integrated with RK4 on the real time deltas. Because the leader never drifts, any error reported below is an error of the follower model alone.

Table 1. The five identified IDM parameters (delta and L_VEH are fixed by the brief, not identified). Fitted by M5; a parameter sitting on a bound means the fit wanted to leave the box.
symbolmeaningvalue for driver_1unitboundsat a bound

Tsafe time headway0.8412s[0.3, 5.0]no

Units. Every quantity stays in the coordinate units (cu) of the recorded trajectory table: x, y, dhw and the spacing in cu, the speeds in cu/s, the accelerations in cu/s². One vehicle length is LVEH = 250 cu by the lab brief. No metre/second conversion is applied anywhere, because none is documented for this dataset (the vehicle-reported velocity column is discarded by stage 4 for exactly that reason: it disagrees with the position-difference speed by roughly a factor of three). The style thresholds of section 5 are therefore stated in the same units, and the one threshold that would need a physical conversion is also given in a unit-free (sigma-relative) form.

3. Calibration

Five identification methods were compared by leave-one-event-out cross-validation: each fold trains on the driver's remaining events and then predicts the held-out event, so the comparison is on data the fit never saw. The ranking score is mean(spacing RMSE)/scale_s + mean(speed RMSE)/scale_v + 1.0 × Σviolations, with the scales the pooled standard deviations of the driver's measured spacing and speed.

Table 4. The five methods and their cross-validation results for driver_1 (★ = the selected method). Lower scores are better. The global methods run at half budget inside the cross-validation because CV multiplies the number of optimisations by the number of folds; the final retrain always uses the full budget.

Why the cross-validation winner is not the lowest-cost fit. The ranking above is built on held-out events, whereas the normalised cost J of the fit set rewards the position of the optimum of the whole set. On this data the two orderings disagree, which is the reason the selection was made by cross-validation in the first place.

4. Validation run

The validation collection data/raw/collection_20260917_144342 is processed by exactly the same four stages as the human data, which puts it in the isolated tree data/preprocess/validation_driver_1/stage_1..4. The parameters of driver_1 are then replayed event by event: initial state = the event's first measured sample, leader input = the measured leader speed, RK4 on the real time deltas.

These validation tables come from a DEMO run. results/validation_driver_1.json was produced with --demo, i.e. the collection named above is a real recording used to stand in for the TA's validation run. 5. Driving style

The style metrics are computed on the measured trajectories only, so the human run and the validation run are described by the same yardstick. They are grouped into efficiency, comfort and safety. Acceleration and jerk come from the measured speed series by central differences with one-sided ends (the convention stage 4 uses for its speeds), so a 0.1 s sampling grid makes them the most noise-sensitive metrics of the three groups.

Table 9. Every threshold used by the style metrics, with the reason it was chosen. All are module constants of src/analysis/metrics.py and are listed here so no comparison rests on an undocumented number.
quantityvaluebasis
stop speedv ≤ 1.0 cu/s1 cu/s, about 0.7 percent of the calibrated free speed (-140 cu/s); a sample at or below it is treated as a standstill
acceleration limits50 cu/s², 100 cu/s², 200 cu/s²50 / 100 / 200 cu/s^2: 50 is metadata.json idm_params.max_accel_per_sec, 100 the midpoint of the calibration box of `a`, 200 its upper end (idm_core.UPPER[3]) and therefore the strongest acceleration the identified model can produce in these units
acceleration sigma levels2.0σa, 3.0σa2 and 3 event sigma_a: unit-free, so it needs no physical conversion and is the criterion used in the style scores
TTC thresholds1.5 s, 3.0 s1.5 s critical and 3.0 s warning, the two thresholds of the usual TTC surrogate-safety literature; TTC is in seconds and therefore unit-free
spacing violations ≤ 0 cus <= 0, the same violation convention idm_core counts during a simulation
reference minimum gap80 cu80 cu, metadata.json idm_params.min_spacing (reported, not scored)
score scalesaccel_cu_s2 = 200, jerk_cu_s3 = 2,000, spacing_cu = 250, ttc_s = 3values at which the normalised 0-1 style scores saturate (see the radar chart)

Automatic conclusions

Generated from the numbers above with a 5 percent materiality band: a relative change smaller than that is reported as agreement rather than as a difference.

  • Mean follower speed: human 117.00 cu/s vs validation 105.48 cu/s - lower by 9.8 percent (higher is better).
  • Speed achievement mean(v)/v0: human 0.837 vs validation 0.755 - lower by 9.8 percent (higher is better).
  • Total driving time: human 24.9 s vs validation 33.8 s - absolute difference +8.9 s (context, not a quality).
  • Stop fraction: 0 in both runs (lower is better).
  • Mean acceleration (signed, near zero): human 3.18 cu/s^2 vs validation -2.85 cu/s^2 - absolute difference -6.04 cu/s^2 (context, not a quality).
  • Acceleration RMS: human 97.84 cu/s^2 vs validation 111.32 cu/s^2 - higher by 13.8 percent (lower is better).
  • Jerk RMS: human 1150.52 cu/s^3 vs validation 1337.66 cu/s^3 - higher by 16.3 percent (lower is better).
  • Minimum spacing: human 124.1 cu vs validation 165.8 cu - higher by 33.5 percent (higher is better).
  • Minimum TTC: human 1.997 s vs validation 3.683 s - higher by 84.4 percent (higher is better).
  • Share of samples below TTC = 1.5 s: 0 in both runs (lower is better).
  • Spacing RMSE of the identified IDM: human 58.6 cu vs validation 72.5 cu - higher by 23.7 percent (lower is better).
  • Speed RMSE of the identified IDM: human 16.91 cu/s vs validation 18.94 cu/s - higher by 12.0 percent (lower is better).
  • Efficiency score: human 0.837 vs validation 0.755 (-0.082) - better on the human run.
  • Comfort score: human 0.511 vs validation 0.443 (-0.067) - better on the human run.
  • Safety score: human 0.581 vs validation 0.832 (+0.250) - better on the validation run.
  • No simulated spacing violation (s <= 0) occurred in either run, so every reported error was produced without clamping.

6. Limitations

  • This report is a DEMO. DEMO - no validation run exists yet. The validation tables of this report come from the human collection data/raw/collection_20260917_144342 (the other driver's recording), pushed through the same stage 1..4 pipeline as if it were the driver_1 validation run. The preprocessing, the IDM replay, the metrics and the figures are the real code paths; only the role of the validation input is simulated, so the model-transfer error visible in section 4 is expected (the parameters of driver_1 are being applied to a trajectory it was never fitted to) and is not a defect of the pipeline. The pipeline and the metrics are the real ones; the validation input is not.
  • Few events. driver_1 contributes 3 event(s) and the cross-validation therefore has 3 fold(s); one event cannot be averaged away, so a single unusual manoeuvre moves the ranking. Every fold trains on the remaining events only, which for this driver is a very small training set.
  • Event length. The events are short (from 14.0 s, 2.6 s, 8.3 s in the human run), so acceleration, jerk and TTC statistics rest on a few hundred samples at 0.1 s spacing.
  • Unit system. All quantities are in coordinate units; no documented conversion to metres exists for this dataset and the vehicle-reported velocity column disagrees with the position-difference speed by about a factor of three, so it is discarded. Physical thresholds are therefore partly given as multiples of the run's own standard deviation (see Table 9).
  • Parameter bounds. No identified parameter sits on a bound for this driver.
  • Driver-1 consistency. The cross-validation of driver_1 is visibly less consistent than that of driver_2 (its mean spacing RMSE and its worst-fold RMSE are several times larger), and several of its folds were infeasible, which is itself evidence that one event of that driver is not described by the parameters the others imply.
  • Leader is an input. The simulation is fed the measured leader speed, so the follower model is never asked to predict the leader; any leader-follower interaction error is invisible here by construction.
  • Metrics from position differences. Speeds are position differences and accelerations and jerks are their differences, so quantisation noise grows with each derivative; the acceleration-based comfort columns are consequently the most uncertain of the report and are why the sigma-relative threshold is reported next to the absolute one.
  • Single validation run. A validation run is one realisation: without repetitions there is no way to separate a systematic difference between the human and the validation driver from the day-to-day spread of a single run.

Generated by src/analysis/build_html_report.py from src/calibrate/cross_validate.py, results/final_params.json, the stage summary JSONs under data/preprocess and data/preprocess/validation_driver_1, plus results/validation_driver_1.json. Figures are rendered by matplotlib and embedded as base64 PNG; the file is fully self-contained and needs no network access. No wall-clock timestamp is written into it, so two runs on the same artifacts are byte-identical.
